Over the next twenty minutes, we will trace how vaccines have transformed public health across two centuries — from Edward Jenner's first smallpox vaccine in 1796 to the record-breaking development of COVID-19 vaccines in 2020. Our focus is on hard data: what vaccines have achieved, where gaps remain, and what global health systems must do next.

Key points: (1) Two-century scope from smallpox to COVID-19 (2) Data-driven analysis from Our World in Data (3) Audience: public health professionals and policy analysts
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 02_vaccine_timeline

[Transition] Let's begin by looking at how the pace of vaccine development has accelerated over time.

The timeline from pathogen identification to vaccine licensure has shortened dramatically. Typhoid fever took 105 years — the pathogen was identified in 1884, but the vaccine wasn't licensed until 1989. Meningitis followed a similar pattern at 92 years. [Pause]

[Data] But look at the bottom of this chart. COVID-19 went from pathogen identification to licensed vaccine in under one year — that is a compression factor of more than 100x compared to typhoid. This was made possible by modern tools: genome sequencing, mRNA technology, and decades of foundational research.

Key points: (1) Early vaccines took decades to over a century (2) COVID-19 achieved licensure in under one year (3) mRNA technology was the key enabler
Duration: 3 minutes

---

# 03_us_disease_elimination

[Transition] That accelerating innovation has delivered extraordinary results. Let's look at the disease reduction data for the United States.

This table shows pre-vaccine versus post-vaccine case and death rates from Roush and Murphy's landmark 2007 study. Three diseases — diphtheria, smallpox, and acute polio — achieved complete 100% elimination of both cases and deaths. [Pause]

[Data] Measles went from over 3,000 cases per million per year down to 0.2 — that is a 99.99% reduction. However, not all diseases show such dramatic results. Pneumococcal disease has seen only a 40.5% reduction in cases and 31.3% in deaths, which we will examine further in a later slide.

Key points: (1) Three diseases fully eliminated (2) Measles nearly eliminated at 99.99% (3) Pneumococcal and hepatitis still show significant burden
Duration: 3 minutes

---

# 04_measles_heatmap

[Transition] To see just how transformative vaccination policy can be, let's zoom in on measles across all 50 US states.

This heatmap shows measles incidence from the 1930s through the 2010s. Before 1963, virtually every state experienced high measles incidence — ranging from 100 to over 1,000 cases per 100,000 people. The landscape transformed through three milestones. [Pause]

In 1963, John Enders developed the first measles vaccine. In 1971, Maurice Hilleman created the combined MMR vaccine. And in 1980, vaccination became mandatory for children entering kindergarten. After that mandate, the heatmap shifts from dark red to near-white across all 50 states. Only sporadic outbreaks have occurred since.

Key points: (1) Three milestone years: 1963, 1971, 1980 (2) Mandatory vaccination was the decisive policy lever (3) Near-zero cases sustained for over four decades
Duration: 3 minutes

---

# 05_smallpox_eradication

[Transition] The measles story is powerful, but the ultimate vaccination success story is smallpox — the only human disease ever eradicated.

The WHO passed a resolution to eradicate smallpox in 1959 and launched an intensified campaign in 1967. By 1977, the last natural case occurred in Somalia. In 1980, eradication was officially certified. [Pause]

Three factors made this uniquely possible. First, smallpox infected only humans — there was no animal reservoir to reintroduce it. Second, symptoms were visually distinguishable, enabling rapid case identification. Third, the vaccine was cheap and highly effective. This combination of biology and public health infrastructure made eradication achievable.

Key points: (1) Eradication certified in 1980 after an 18-year intensive campaign (2) Three enabling factors: human-only host, visible symptoms, effective vaccine (3) Remains the only disease ever eradicated through vaccination
Duration: 3 minutes

---

# 06_herd_immunity

[Transition] Smallpox eradication illustrates a broader principle: vaccines protect not just individuals, but entire communities through herd immunity.

This diagram shows three scenarios. Without vaccination, pathogens spread freely and vulnerable individuals are infected. With partial vaccination, some spread still occurs. But when enough people are vaccinated — herd immunity — pathogens simply cannot find enough susceptible hosts to sustain transmission. [Pause]

This matters most for those who cannot be vaccinated: newborns who are too young, immunocompromised individuals whose immune systems are too weak, and cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy. These groups depend entirely on the vaccinated population surrounding them for protection.

Key points: (1) Herd immunity blocks pathogen transmission at the population level (2) Protects the most vulnerable: newborns, immunocompromised, cancer patients (3) Requires sufficient vaccination coverage to be effective
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 07_remaining_challenges

[Transition] However, we must be honest about where we have not yet succeeded.

Pneumococcal disease has seen only a 40.5% reduction in cases and just 31.3% in deaths — far from the 100% elimination achieved for diphtheria and polio. Hepatitis A shows 89% case reduction, and acute hepatitis B stands at 83.9%. These numbers represent real, ongoing disease burden. [Pause]

Three barriers explain the gap. First, global access remains unequal — not everyone has access to vaccines. Second, supply shortages put children at risk, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Third, poor scientific understanding reduces trust and vaccine uptake in many communities. Addressing these barriers requires systemic investment.

Key points: (1) Pneumococcal at only 40.5% case reduction is the widest gap (2) Three systemic barriers: access, supply, and trust (3) Closing these gaps requires targeted investment and policy action
Duration: 3 minutes

---

# 08_takeaways

[Transition] Let me bring together the five key findings from this analysis.

First, vaccines have achieved 100% elimination of diphtheria, smallpox, and polio in the United States. Second, development timelines have collapsed from over a century to under one year, thanks to mRNA technology. Third, measles cases dropped to near zero across all 50 states after the 1980 mandate. Fourth, smallpox remains the only human disease ever eradicated through vaccination. And fifth, significant gaps persist for pneumococcal disease, hepatitis A, and hepatitis B. [Pause]

The call to action is clear: expand global vaccine access, invest in next-generation vaccines to close the remaining gaps, and build public trust through better scientific communication and community engagement. The data shows what vaccines can achieve — our task is to finish the job.

Key points: (1) Five evidence-based takeaways (2) Three priority actions for global health systems (3) The tools exist; the challenge is implementation
Duration: 2 minutes

Key points: (1) Pneumococcal at only 40.5% case reduction is the widest gap (2) Three systemic barriers: access, supply, and trust (3) Closing these gaps requires targeted investment and policy action
Duration: 3 minutes

---

# 08_takeaways

[Transition] Let me bring together the five key findings from this analysis.

First, vaccines have achieved 100% elimination of diphtheria, smallpox, and polio in the United States. Second, development timelines have collapsed from over a century to under one year, thanks to mRNA technology. Third, measles cases dropped to near zero across all 50 states after the 1980 mandate. Fourth, smallpox remains the only human disease ever eradicated through vaccination. And fifth, significant gaps persist for pneumococcal disease, hepatitis A, and hepatitis B. [Pause]

The call to action is clear: expand global vaccine access, invest in next-generation vaccines to close the remaining gaps, and build public trust through better scientific communication and community engagement. The data shows what vaccines can achieve — our task is to finish the job.

Key points: (1) Five evidence-based takeaways (2) Three priority actions for global health systems (3) The tools exist; the challenge is implementation
Duration: 2 minutes
